Silva used the mosaic theory - combining non-material nonpublic information with the industry expert's report - to reach his conclusion, which is permissible.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The CFO's information was nonpublic but not material - a general statement about the company's financial condition that would not by itself affect the stock price - and Silva did not trade solely on it, so there is no violation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Members may compensate individuals for their insights. The industry report is available to anyone who pays for it and is based on point-of-sale data, so it is not material nonpublic information; using it is not a violation.

questions.module: Application of the Code and Standards
questions.los: Application of the Code and Standards: V(C) Record Retention (格式与年限)
questions.stem: Does Silva violate the Standards with respect to record retention?

choices.B: Yes, because of the format in which the records are kept
choices.C: Yes, because records must be retained for a minimum period of 7 years

explanations.A: Correct. Silva did not violate Standard V(C) Record Retention. Records may be kept in hard copy or electronic form, and firms may set the applicable time frame. Because local regulations require 5-year retention and Silva retains records for 5 years, he complies.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Standard V(C) does not require a specific format; records may be kept in hard copy or electronic form.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Standard V(C) does not mandate 7-year retention. The 7-year minimum is only a recommendation in the absence of regulatory or firm guidance; here local regulation requires 5 years, which Silva meets.

questions.module: Application of the Code and Standards
questions.los: Application of the Code and Standards: I(C) Misrepresentation (来源引用 / 前雇员模型归属)
questions.stem: To comply with the Standards in his research on Company A, Murphy must cite:

choices.C: both Jones and the data providers.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Murphy must cite the data providers but is not required to cite Jones. Research and models developed while employed by a firm are the property of the firm, which may issue future reports without attributing prior analysts.
explanations.B: Correct. Under Standard I(C) Misrepresentation, preparing research from multiple sources without acknowledging them is a violation; members must give credit where due and reveal sources of forecasts and data. Murphy must cite the external data providers. He need not cite Jones, whose model is now firm property and who has left the firm.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Murphy must cite the data providers, but citing Jones is not required - models developed while employed at the firm belong to the firm, which may use them without attributing the departed analyst.

questions.module: Application of the Code and Standards
questions.los: Application of the Code and Standards: II(B) Market Manipulation (intent 是否存在)
questions.stem: Does Gaskill violate the Standard relating to market manipulation with her interviews and speaking engagements?

choices.B: Yes, by engaging in information-based manipulation
choices.C: Yes, by engaging in transaction-based manipulation

explanations.A: Correct. Gaskill does not violate Standard II(B) Market Manipulation. Market manipulation involves disseminating false or misleading information or transactions intended to deceive; intent is critical. There is no evidence Gaskill spread false information or that trades were intended to distort prices.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Information-based manipulation requires dissemination of false or misleading information; there is no evidence Gaskill did so.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Transaction-based manipulation requires transactions intended to distort the price-setting mechanism; Standard II(B) does not preclude legitimate strategies, and there is no evidence of intent to distort prices.

questions.module: Application of the Code and Standards
questions.los: Application of the Code and Standards: III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality (former client)
questions.stem: Does Bass violate the Standard relating to preservation of confidentiality at the family picnic?

choices.B: Yes, in relation to his former client only
choices.C: Yes, in relation to both his current clients and his former client

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bass violates Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality by naming his former client. The Standard protects client information even after the relationship ends.
explanations.B: Correct. Standard III(E) requires preserving the confidentiality of information from clients, prospective clients, and former clients, and it continues to apply after the relationship ends. By confirming and naming his former client, Bass violates Standard III(E) with respect to that former client.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Bass does not name his current clients or discuss their finances; describing the general profile of clients he serves is not a breach. He violates the Standard only with respect to the former client he named.

questions.module: Application of the Code and Standards
questions.los: Application of the Code and Standards: IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors (激励与授权)
questions.stem: Does Murphy's supervisor violate the Standards in his oversight of the department?

explanations.A: Correct. Neither policy violates Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors. Offering incentives - monetary or otherwise - to reward ethical behavior is an acceptable way to assist employees in meeting their obligations, and supervisors of large numbers of employees may delegate supervisory duties to properly trained subordinates.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Monetary incentives to reward ethical behavior do not violate Standard IV(C); they help employees comply with their legal and ethical obligations.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Delegating supervisory responsibility to a trained deputy does not violate Standard IV(C). Members with oversight of large numbers of employees may delegate to subordinates who directly oversee the others.

questions.module: Application of the Code and Standards
questions.los: Application of the Code and Standards: III(A) Loyalty/Prudence/Care (best execution / proxy voting)
questions.stem: Does Dines violate the Standards in the initial meeting with Kagan?

choices.B: Yes, regarding her proxy voting policy
choices.C: Yes, regarding the broker for Kagan's account

explanations.A: Incorrect. Dines violates Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care by not acting in the client's best interest - she failed to inform Kagan that his preferred broker may not provide best execution.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Dines does not violate the Standards regarding proxy voting. Voting proxies is part of the duty of loyalty, but a cost-benefit analysis may show that voting all proxies does not benefit the client; members should disclose their proxy voting policies, which Dines did.
explanations.C: Correct. Under Standard III(A), members must place clients' interests first and seek best execution. In a directed brokerage situation the manager should inform the client that they may not be getting best execution. Kagan's preferred broker is clearly not the best execution option, and Dines failed to inform him, violating Standard III(A).

questions.module: Application of the Code and Standards
questions.los: Application of the Code and Standards: III(B) Fair Dealing (客户下单与当前推荐相反)
questions.stem: Does Dines violate the Standards in her actions related to Cromwell?

choices.B: Yes, because of her actions related to the buy order for Kagan's account
choices.C: Yes, because of her actions related to setting up calls with the senior analyst

explanations.A: Incorrect. Dines violates Standard III(B) Fair Dealing. She did not violate it by arranging analyst calls only for premium clients, but she did violate it by not informing Kagan of the changed Cromwell recommendation before executing his buy order.
explanations.B: Correct. Under Standard III(B) Fair Dealing, if clients place orders contrary to a current recommendation, they should be advised of the changed recommendation before the order is accepted. Because Prism had changed its rating to a sell, Kagan should have been informed before his buy order was executed. Failing to do so - even though Kagan is a sector expert - violates the Standard.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dines is not required to offer premium services to all clients and did not provide advance information. Fair dealing means dealing fairly, not equally; she waited until after publication to set up the premium-client calls, which is permissible.

questions.module: Application of the Code and Standards
questions.los: Application of the Code and Standards: III(D) Performance Presentation (代表性账户 / 加权复合)
questions.stem: Dines violates the Standards in her performance presentation for Kagan with regard to:

choices.B: the disclosure of taxes and fees only.
choices.C: both the account sample and the disclosure of taxes and fees.

explanations.A: Correct. Under Standard III(D) Performance Presentation, communications must be fair, accurate, and complete. Presenting only the top and bottom decile of accounts gives an inaccurate and incomplete picture of the strategy's overall performance; a weighted-average composite of similar portfolios should be used. Using selected accounts is the violation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The tax and fee disclosure is compliant. Disclosures should fully explain the results (e.g., gross of fees, before taxes), which this disclosure does; net returns would vary by each client's fees and tax status.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dines violates Standard III(D) with respect to the account sample (using only two deciles rather than a weighted composite) but not with respect to the tax/fee disclosure.

questions.module: Application of the Code and Standards
questions.los: Application of the Code and Standards: IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements (bonus 已获批 vs 游艇未披露)
questions.stem: Does Dines violate the Standards with respect to either Kagan's bonus offer or the use of his yacht?

choices.B: Yes, with respect to Kagan's bonus offer
choices.C: Yes, with respect to the use of Kagan's yacht

explanations.A: Incorrect. Dines violates Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements by not disclosing the yacht arrangement. She does not violate with respect to the profit share because she informed her employer and obtained permission.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Dines does not violate Standard IV(B) by accepting the share of profits. She obtained written permission from her employer, so the bonus arrangement is compliant even though it is a direct share of client profits.
explanations.C: Correct. Under Standard IV(B), members must not accept gifts, benefits, or consideration that might create a conflict of interest with the employer's interest without written consent from all parties. Although the yacht is not monetary compensation, it could create a conflict (favoring Kagan over other clients) and should have been reported to the employer for consent before accepting. By not informing her employer, Dines violates Standard IV(B).

questions.los: Credit migration: expected return under a transition matrix
questions.stem: The expected 1-year total return for the Don Vallejo A-rated bond under Jackson’s credit migration scenario is closest to:

explanations.A: See correct answer B.
explanations.B: B is correct because the expected total return of the A-rated bond is the sum of the YTM and the expected percentage change in bond value. The YTM is 1%, while the expected return due to a credit spread change can be computed as (minus) the expected spread change (subject to migration) times the modified duration of the bond of 4.5. In turn, the expected spread change for an A-rated bond is the probability-weighted spread change, where the probabilities are retrieved from the transition matrix row with the label rating of "A". We first compute the expected percentage price change using the modified duration of 4.5 for each rating migration. From A to AAA: –4.5 × –0.5% = 2.25%; From A to AA: –4.5 × –0.3% = 1.35%; From A to A: –4.5 × 0% = 0%; From A to BBB: –4.5 × 0.4% = –1.8%; From A to BB: –4.5 × 0.6% = –2.7%; From A to B: –4.5 × 0.8% = –3.6%; From A to CCC: –4.5 × 1.5% = –6.75%. The expected price return is computed by multiplying each price change by the appropriate probability from the transition matrix in the row with the label rating of "A". Expected price return = 2.25% × 0.02 + 1.35% × 0.03 + 0% × 0.88 – 1.8% × 0.02 – 2.7% × 0.02 – 3.6% × 0.02 – 6.75% × 0.01 = –0.144%. The expected total return of the bond is therefore: –0.144% + 1% = 0.856%, which is rounded to 0.86%.
explanations.C: See correct answer B.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: Expected total return = YTM + expected % price change; expected % price change = Σ [ (–ModDur × Δspread) × migration probability ] using the A-rating row

steps.label: 结果
steps.content: Expected price return = –0.144%; total return = –0.144% + 1% = 0.856% ≈ 0.86%

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: Use the row of the CURRENT rating (A) for probabilities; add the 1% YTM back to the price effect.

questions.los: Credit analysis approaches for structured finance (loan-by-loan / portfolio / statistics-based)
questions.stem: The most suitable approach for the credit analysis of the commercial ABS is:

explanations.A: A is incorrect because a loan-by-loan approach is not suitable when the portfolio is granular and homogeneous. Evaluating each loan on an individual basis is too time-consuming and therefore it is not suitable in this case. A loan-by-loan approach would be inefficient because of the large number of basically similar loans.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because a portfolio-based approach is not suitable when the portfolio of loans is short-term, as the portfolio does not materially change in the short term. Short-term structured finance vehicles with granular, homogeneous assets tend to be evaluated using a statistics-based approach to the existing book of loans. A portfolio-based approach is instead more suitable when the portfolio of loans is medium-term/dynamic and therefore subject to change over time.
explanations.C: C is correct because short-term structured finance vehicles with granular, homogeneous assets tend to be evaluated using a statistics-based approach to the existing book of loans. A statistics-based approach is most suitable when the portfolio of loans is short-term (and therefore fairly static), granular, and homogeneous, like in this case. Portfolio statistics are sufficient to appropriately analyze the credit of the loan pool.

questions.los: CDS settlement: cheapest-to-deliver and combined position proceeds
questions.stem: At settlement of the Electric Motors CDS, the total proceeds from Jackson’s Bond X and CDS positions are:

explanations.A: See correct answer C.
explanations.B: See correct answer C.
explanations.C: C is correct because Jackson holds a $20 million position in Bond X, and simultaneously has bought protection using a CDS contract referencing Electric Motors. Upon default, the value of the position is computed as follows: The position on Bond X is valued $20 million × 40% = $8 million. The payoff on the CDS contract is $20 million × 65% = $13 million. The cheapest-to-deliver (CTD) contract is the one which shall be chosen to deliver. As Bond Y trades at 35% of face value while Bond X trades at 40% of face value, Bond Y is the CTD contract and therefore the recovery rate of the CDS contract is 65%. The total proceeds from the combined position are therefore $8 million + $13 million = $21 million.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: Total proceeds = value of Bond X held + CDS payoff; CDS payoff = notional × (1 – recovery of CTD)

steps.label: 代入
steps.content: Bond X = $20m × 40% = $8m; CTD is Bond Y at 35% → recovery = 35%, so payoff = $20m × (1–35%) = $20m × 65% = $13m

steps.label: 结果
steps.content: $8m + $13m = $21 million

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: CDS payoff uses the cheapest-to-deliver (lowest price = Bond Y at 35%), not the bond actually held (Bond X at 40%).

questions.los: CDS curve trades: profiting from an expected flattening
questions.stem: Which of the following strategies should profit the most from the expected flattening of the Crispy Chips CDS curve?

explanations.A: A is incorrect because, as the Crispy Chips CDS curve is expected to flatten, Jackson should sell protection using the 5-year contract in order to maximize the gains from a tightening of long-term CDS spreads. On the contrary, buying protection using the 1-year contract minimizes the losses from widening of short-term CDS spreads. Strategy 1 incorrectly suggests that selling protection is profitable when CDS spreads increase (rather than decrease), and conversely that buying protection is profitable when CDS spreads decrease (rather than increase).
explanations.B: B is incorrect because, as the Crispy Chips CDS curve is expected to flatten, Jackson should sell protection using the 5-year contract in order to maximize the gains from a tightening of long-term CDS spreads. On the contrary, buying protection using the 3-year contract is not the best strategy—losses are minimized when Jackson buys protection using the 1-year contract rather than the 3-year contract. Strategy 2 is not the one which Jackson should implement, as Strategy 3 is more profitable.
explanations.C: C is correct because, as the Crispy Chips CDS curve is expected to flatten, Jackson should sell protection using the 5-year contract in order to maximize the gains from a tightening of long-term CDS spreads. On the contrary, buying protection using the 1-year contract minimizes the losses from widening of short-term CDS spreads. Put differently, protection at the short end is expected to become more expensive, so he should buy it now, while protection at the long end is becoming cheaper, so he should sell it now. Strategy 3 is the one which Jackson should implement as it yields the maximum profit, should Jackson's expected flattening of the CDS curve materialize.

questions.los: Foreign currency transaction gain/loss on a monetary item
questions.stem: The foreign currency transaction gain (in UYU millions) on exported goods reported by Celeste in the most recent year is closest to:

explanations.A: See correct answer C.
explanations.B: See correct answer C.
explanations.C: C is correct because for foreign currency transactions whose settlement dates fall in subsequent accounting periods, both IFRS and US GAAP require adjustments to reflect intervening changes in currency exchange rates. Foreign currency transaction gain and losses are reported on the income statement. As the export receivable is in USD and the USD appreciated against the UYP from 15 November (42.95 UYU/USD) to 31 December (44.63 UYU/USD), the receivable that remains outstanding as of 31 December generates a foreign transaction gain of: Foreign transaction gain = USD 5 million (44.63 – 42.95) = UYU 8.4 million

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: Transaction gain = FC receivable × (rate at year-end – rate at transaction date)

steps.label: 结果
steps.content: = USD 5 million × 1.68 = UYU 8.4 million

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: Use transaction-date rate (15 Nov 42.95) not the 1 Jan or average rate; the USD receivable gains as USD appreciates.

questions.los: Current rate method: translating revenue and cost of sales at the average rate
questions.stem: Salto’s contribution to Celeste’s consolidated gross profit (in UYU millions) in the most recent year is closest to:

explanations.A: A is correct because Celeste uses the current rate method to translate Salto’s financial statements. Under such methods, revenues and expenses are translated at the exchange rate that existed when the transaction took place. For practical reasons, a rate that approximates the exchange rates at the dates of the transactions, such as an average exchange rate, may be used. Therefore, Salto’s translated gross profit (Salto’s contribution to Celeste’s consolidated gross profit) in the most recent year is: Gross profit = Revenue (USD) × Average exchange rate – Cost of sales (USD) × Average exchange rate; Gross profit = USD 120 million × 43.26 – USD 65 million × 43.26 = UYU 2,379.3 million ~ UYU 2,379
explanations.B: See correct answer A.
explanations.C: See correct answer A.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: Under the current rate method, revenue and COGS are translated at the average rate: Gross profit = (Rev – COS) × average rate

steps.label: 结果
steps.content: = UYU 2,379.3 million ≈ UYU 2,379

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: Current rate method uses the average rate (43.26), NOT the 42.81 inventory-purchase rate (that historical rate is used only under the temporal method).

questions.los: Temporal vs. current rate method: effect on total shareholders’ equity
questions.stem: If Monte's results had been translated using the current rate method, its total shareholders' equity would have been:

explanations.A: A is incorrect because the method Celeste used to translate Monte’s financial statements (temporal method) resulted in total shareholders’ equity that was lower than it would have been under the current rate method.
explanations.B: See correct answer C.
explanations.C: C is correct because Celeste uses the temporal method to translate Monte’s financial statements. Under this method, monetary assets and liabilities (in USD) are translated at the current exchange rate, non-monetary assets and liabilities measured at historical cost (in USD) are translated at historical exchange rates. Monte’s monetary assets and liabilities were translated using the end-of-year exchange rate (44.63 UYU/USD). Monte’s non-monetary assets (the only non-monetary assets are inventory and fixed assets, and all liabilities are monetary) were translated using the average exchange rate prevailing at time of purchase (42.15 UYU/USD). This last exchange rate is lower than the end-of-year exchange rate. If Celeste had used the method used for Salto to translate Monte’s financial statements (the current rate method), all assets and liabilities (in USD) would have been translated (into UYU) at the current exchange rate at balance sheet date (44.63 UYU/USD). Therefore, the method Celeste used to translate Monte’s financial statements (temporal method) resulted in total shareholders’ equity that was lower than it would have been under the current rate method.

questions.los: Hyperinflationary economy translation under IFRS (IAS 29 restate then current rate)
questions.stem: Is Romano correct about the method that Celeste should use to translate the new subsidiary’s financial statements?

choices.B: No, because Celeste should use the temporal method
choices.C: No, because Celeste should use the average exchange rate for the income statement

explanations.A: A is correct because when a foreign entity is located in a highly inflationary economy IFRS requires that the foreign entity’s financial statements first be restated for local inflation using the procedures outlined in IAS 29. Then, the inflation-restated foreign currency financial statements are translated into the parent’s presentation currency using the current exchange rate. Therefore, Romano is correct about the method that Celeste should use to translate the new subsidiary’s financial statements.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because Celeste should use the method indicated by Romano to translate the new subsidiary’s financial statements, and not the temporal method.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because Celeste should use the method indicated by Romano to translate the new subsidiary’s financial statements. This method uses the current exchange rate as of year-end both for the balance sheet and the income statement.

questions.los: Cash-flow-based accruals ratio
questions.stem: Apex's cash-flow-based accruals ratio for the year just ended is closest to:

explanations.A: See correct answer C.
explanations.B: See correct answer C.
explanations.C: C is correct because the cash flow accruals ratio for the year just ended is 11% as follows: = [NI1 − (CFO1 + CFI1)] / [(NOA1 + NOA0) / 2] where: NI = net income; CFO = cash flow from operations; CFI = cash flow from investing; NOA = net operating assets. = [83 − [113 + (–58)]] / [(280 + 229) / 2] = [83 − (55)] / [(509) / 2] = 28 / 254.5 ≈ 11%

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: Cash-flow-based accruals ratio = [NI – (CFO + CFI)] / [average NOA]

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: CFI is negative (–58), so CFO + CFI = 55; denominator is AVERAGE NOA, not ending NOA.

questions.los: Effect of reclassifying inventory to non-current assets on ratios
questions.stem: As a result of Apex's reclassification of its inventory in the year that has just ended, which of the following ratios most likely increased?

explanations.A: A is incorrect because Apex's reclassifies its inventory, which is part of current assets, to other non-current assets therefore the current ratio will decrease because current assets will decrease and current liabilities will stay the same.
explanations.B: B is correct because the inventory turnover calculated using the reported inventory number will most likely increase because the amount of inventory relative to cost of goods sold will decrease.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because the number of days of inventory on hand calculated using the reported inventory number will most likely decrease because the amount of inventory relative to cost of goods sold will decrease.

questions.los: Accounting for a controlling equity investment (acquisition method)
questions.stem: Apex should account for its purchase of Beast using the:

explanations.A: A is incorrect because if Apex is deemed to have control over Beast, it would use the acquisition method to account for Beast in its consolidated financial statements. The equity method is used for some joint ventures and when there is significant influence but not control. In this case, Apex has an 80% stake and has control over Beast.
explanations.B: B is correct because if Apex is deemed to have control over Beast, it would use the acquisition method to account for Beast in its consolidated financial statements. In this case, Apex has an 80% stake and has control over Beast.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because if Apex is deemed to have control over Beast, it would use the acquisition method to account for Beast in its consolidated financial statements. Proportionate consolidation is used for joint ventures. In this case, Apex has an 80% stake and has control over Beast.

questions.los: Full goodwill method (US GAAP)
questions.stem: As a result of its purchase of Beast, Apex should recognize goodwill of:

explanations.A: See correct answer B.
explanations.B: B is correct because Apex reports under US GAAP, and should report $5 million under the full goodwill method. Full goodwill = Fair value of entity – Fair value of identifiable net assets = $30 million – $25 million = $5 million.
explanations.C: See correct answer B.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: Full goodwill (US GAAP) = Fair value of entire entity – Fair value of identifiable net assets

steps.label: 代入
steps.content: = $30 million – $25 million

steps.label: 结果
steps.content: = $5 million

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: US GAAP requires FULL goodwill: use fair value of the whole entity ($30m), not the $24m purchase price of the 80% stake.

questions.los: Residual income = Net income – equity charge
questions.stem: The residual income for LuftComm is closest to:

explanations.A: A is correct because LuftComm’s residual income of €122 million can be calculated using net income and the equity charge (Residual Income = Net Income – Equity Charge) or using net operating profit after taxes and the total capital charge (NOPAT = EBIT × (1 – Tax rate)). Option 1 – Using Net Income and the Equity Charge (€ millions): EBIT 700; Less Interest Expense (180); = Pretax Income 520; Less Income Taxes (78); = Net Income 442. Equity Charge = Book Value of Equity × Cost of Equity = (Book Value of Assets – Book Value of Debt) × Cost of Equity = (5,000 – 3,000) × 0.16 = 320. Residual Income = Net Income – Equity Charge = 442 – 320 = 122. Option 2 – Using NOPAT and the Total Capital Charge (€ millions): NOPAT = EBIT × (1 – Tax Rate) = 700 × (1 – 0.15) = 595. Debt Charge = Book Value of Debt × Pretax Cost of Debt × (1 – Tax Rate) = 3,000 × 0.06 × (1 – 0.15) = 153. Equity Charge = (5,000 – 3,000) × 0.16 = 320. Total Capital Charge = 153 + 320 = 473. Residual Income = NOPAT – Total Capital Charge = 595 – 473 = 122.
explanations.B: See correct answer A.
explanations.C: See correct answer A.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: Residual Income = Net Income – Equity Charge; Equity Charge = (Assets – Debt) × Cost of equity

steps.label: 代入
steps.content: Net Income: EBIT 700 – interest (3,000×6%=180) = 520 pretax; – taxes (520×15%=78) = 442. Equity Charge = (5,000–3,000)×0.16 = 320

steps.label: 结果
steps.content: Residual Income = 442 – 320 = €122 million

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: Interest expense = pretax cost of debt × book debt (180); equity charge uses book equity = assets – debt, not total assets.

questions.los: Single-stage RI model: solving for implied earnings growth
questions.stem: Based on the single-stage residual income model, the implied growth rate of earnings for LuftComm is closest to:

explanations.A: See correct answer B.
explanations.B: B is correct because the implied growth rate of earnings from the single-stage residual income model is calculated by solving for g in the following equation: V0 = B0 + B0[(ROE – r)/ (r – g)] which gives the following: g = r – [((ROE – r) × B0)/ (V0 – B0)]. Book value per share can be calculated using the given price-to-book ratio and market price per share as follows: Book value per share (B0) = Market price per share/Price-to-book ratio = 44.65 / 1.90 = 23.50. Using the market price per share (44.65) as V0, the book value (23.50) as B0, the ROE (22.1%), and the cost of equity (16%) as r, the implied growth rate (g) can be solved as follows: g = r – [((ROE – r) × B0) / (V0 – B0)] = 0.160 – [((0.221 – 0.160) × 23.50) / (44.65 – 23.50)] = 0.09222 ≈ 9.2%
explanations.C: See correct answer B.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: From V0 = B0 + B0[(ROE – r)/(r – g)], solve g = r – [((ROE – r) × B0)/(V0 – B0)]

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: Derive B0 from price ÷ P/B (23.50), not the €44.65 price; V0 is the market price.

questions.los: Persistence factor determinants
questions.stem: Relative to the industry, the persistence factor used in the preliminary report on PrimaNet is most consistent with the firm having:

explanations.A: A is incorrect because PrimaNet’s persistence is lower than the industry average, which is inconsistent with low dividend payouts. Instead, low dividend payout is associated with higher residual income persistence.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because PrimaNet’s persistence is lower than the industry average, which is inconsistent with low levels of accounting rates of return (ROE). Instead, high or extreme levels of accounting return (ROE) are associated with lower residual income persistence.
explanations.C: C is correct because the persistence factor utilized in the preliminary report on PrimaNet is significantly lower than the industry average. High or extreme levels of accounting accruals is consistent with lower residual income persistence.

questions.los: Finite-horizon multistage RI model with premium terminal value
questions.stem: Based on the finite-horizon multistage residual income model, PrimaNet's intrinsic value per share is closest to:

explanations.A: A is correct because the intrinsic value per share of €24.91 is calculated by adding the present value of residual income in Year 1, present value of income in Year 2, and the present value of the terminal value (premium of market value over book value) at the end of Year 2. Where: V0 = Intrinsic value per share today; B0 = Book value per share today = €18.50 in Exhibit 2. The middle term is the sum of the present values of residual income for each year of the forecast period = €2.25 for Year 1 and €2.00 for Year 2. PT = market price at the end of the forecast period = €26.50; BT = book value at the end of the forecast period = €23.75; r = cost of equity = 12.8%. V0 = 18.50 + 2.25 + 2.00 + [(26.50 - 23.75) / (1.128)2] = €24.91
explanations.B: See correct answer A.
explanations.C: See correct answer A.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: V0 = B0 + Σ PV(residual income) + PV of terminal premium; terminal premium = (PT – BT)/(1+r)^T

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: RI values are already present values (add directly); discount only the terminal premium (PT–BT) at the cost of equity, not WACC.

questions.module: The Term Structure and Interest Rate Dynamics
questions.los: YTM of a coupon bond vs. the spot curve
questions.stem: The current yield to maturity (YTM) on a default-free, 1.2% annual-pay, three-year coupon bond is closest to:

explanations.A: See correct answer B.
explanations.B: B is correct because the YTM on a three-year coupon bond will be closest to the three-year spot rate, regardless of coupon. The three-year spot rate is 1.45%. The price of the bond is calculated as the present value of cash flows. PV = PMT/(1 + z1)1 + PMT/(1 +z2)2 + PMT + 100/(1 + z3)3, Where PMT = coupon and z = spot rate for each time period. PV = 1.2/1.0075+1.2/1.0122+101.2/1.01453 = 1.19107 + 1.17171 + 96.9224 = 99.2852. Next, solve for YTM: PV = –99.2852, FV=100, n=3, PMT=1.2 and solving for I/Y = YTM = 1.445% ≈ 1.45%.
explanations.C: See correct answer B.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: Price the bond off the spot curve, then solve for the single YTM that reprices it; YTM ≈ the 3-year spot rate

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: The YTM lands near the 3-year spot rate (1.45%), not the coupon (1.2%) or the forward f(3,1)=2.25%.

questions.module: The Term Structure and Interest Rate Dynamics
questions.los: Rolling down the curve: return equals the forward rate when the curve is unchanged
questions.stem: Given Eng's expectation for spot rates, the first-year return on a 3-year zero-coupon bond is closest to:

explanations.A: See correct answer C.
explanations.B: See correct answer C.
explanations.C: C is correct because under Eng's spot curve expectation the total return will be the one-year forward rate for year 3. We can see that if the spot rate curve is unchanged, then each bond rolls down the curve and earns the forward rate. This can be shown mathematically by calculating the price of a 3-year zero coupon bond today. Price = 1/(1 + spot rate)3 = 1/(1.01453) = 0.957732. With an unchanged yield curve, this bond will become a 2-year zero coupon bond in one year with a price = 1/(1 + spot rate)2 = 1/(1.01202) = 0.976425. The first year return = 0.976425/0.957732 – 1 ≈ 1.95%, which equals f(2,1) from Exhibit 1.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: With an unchanged spot curve, a 1-year holding-period return on a zero equals the relevant 1-year forward rate f(2,1)

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: The bond rolls from the 3-year to the 2-year spot; the roll return equals f(2,1)=1.95%, not the 3-year spot 1.45%.

questions.module: The Term Structure and Interest Rate Dynamics
questions.los: Term structure theories: segmented markets
questions.stem: Client 1's restriction regarding the securities Eng can purchase is most consistent with the assumptions underlying the:

explanations.A: A is incorrect because the preferred habitat theory postulates that if the expected additional returns to be gained become large enough, institutions will be willing to deviate from their preferred maturities or habitats. Eng is not able to do that due to his investor-imposed constraints.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because the liquidity preference theory focuses on investor's risk aversion and the fact that they demand a liquidity premium for added interest rate risk. Eng would prefer to invest in longer-term maturities to capture this premium but cannot. Also, Client 1 does not direct Eng to purchase only three-year maturity bonds to capture a possible liquidity premium, but that Eng can purchase securities up to three years. This direction indicates the client does not have a preference to capture the liquidity premium if it exists. Liquidity preference theory asserts that liquidity premiums exist to compensate investors for the added interest rate risk they face when lending long term and that these premiums increase with maturity.
explanations.C: C is correct because due to the direction from the Client, Eng continues to invest only in 3-year maturities even though he expects 5-year maturities to offer superior expected returns. The segmented markets theory assumes that market participants are either unwilling or unable to invest in anything other than securities of their preferred maturity. It follows that the yield of securities of a particular maturity is determined entirely by the supply and demand for funds of that particular maturity.

questions.module: The Term Structure and Interest Rate Dynamics
questions.los: Key rate durations sum to effective duration
questions.stem: The 5-year key rate duration for Client 2's portfolio is closest to:

explanations.A: See correct answer B.
explanations.B: B is correct because for Portfolio 2 the sum of the three portfolio key rate durations must equal the portfolio's effective duration. Effective duration = 1-year key rate duration + 3-year key rate duration + 5-year key rate duration = 3.20 = 0.25 + 1.10 + 5-year key rate duration. 5-year key rate duration = 3.20 – 0.25 – 1.10 = 1.85. Key rate duration measures the portfolio risk exposure to each key rate. If all the key rates move by the same amount, then the yield curve has made a parallel shift, and as a result, the proportional change in value has to be consistent with effective duration.
explanations.C: See correct answer B.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: Sum of key rate durations = effective duration

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: The individual key rate durations must sum to effective duration (a parallel shift); solve for the missing one.

questions.module: Valuation and Analysis of Bonds with Embedded Options
questions.los: Effect of higher interest rate volatility on a putable bond
questions.stem: Under Bisht’s volatility scenario, the value of the putable bond would most likely:

explanations.A: A is incorrect because under a scenario where interest rate volatility is assumed to be higher, the value of the putable bond increases. The value of the putable bond is the i) value of a similar straight bond plus the ii) value of the put option. Therefore, with higher interest rate volatility, the value of the put option increases, causing the overall value of the putable bond to increase and not decrease.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because the value of any embedded option, regardless of the type of option, increases with interest rate volatility and hence impacts the value of the bond.
explanations.C: C is correct because under a scenario where interest rate volatility is assumed to be higher, the value of the putable bond increases. The value of the putable bond is the i) value of a similar straight bond plus the ii) value of the put option. Therefore, with higher interest rate volatility, the value of the put option increases, causing the overall value of the putable bond to increase.

questions.module: Valuation and Analysis of Bonds with Embedded Options
questions.los: Choosing key rate duration for a non-parallel shift
questions.stem: Based on his interest rate scenario, which of the following types of duration would be most appropriate for Bisht to use in evaluating the putable bond?

explanations.A: A is correct because the key rate durations reflect the sensitivity of the bond’s price to change in specific maturities on the benchmark yield curve. Thus, key rate durations help identify the ‘shaping risk’ for bonds—that is, the bond’s sensitivity to changes with the shape of the yield curve (e.g., steepening and flattening). In this case, the interest rate scenario is for a non-parallel shift in the yield curve with only the 2-year benchmark rate changing.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because the effective duration indicates the sensitivity of the bond’s price to a parallel shift of the benchmark yield curve - normally calculated by averaging the changes resulting from shifting the benchmark yield curve up and down by the same amount and not change in one-specific maturity. Effective duration is less appropriate for measuring sensitivity to non-parallel shifts as in this case.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because one-sided duration is the effective duration when interest rates go up or down and are better at capturing the interest rate sensitivity of a callable or putable bond than the normal effective durations, as the upside is capped in the callable bond and down-side is capped in the putable bond. However, since the measure is based on effective duration, it is still based on a parallel shift in the yield curve and not non-parallel shift as per the case here.

questions.module: Market-Based Valuation: Price and Enterprise Value Multiples
questions.los: Trailing vs. forward P/E and rising earnings
questions.stem: Which of the following would best explain the difference between the two Xita P/E ratios in Albertson's previous report?

choices.C: An estimated stock value below the current market price

explanations.A: A is correct because for companies with rising earnings, the forward P/E will be smaller than the trailing P/E because the denominator in the forward P/E calculation will be larger. In the previous report, Xita had a forward P/E ratio of 14.9 and a trailing P/E ratio of 15.7, which is consistent with rising earnings at the company.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because with the numerator (current stock price) being the same in both ratios, any difference between the trailing and forward P/E ratios must arise from differences in earnings per share. Any expected increase in earnings, even if positive growth was slower than forecast, will result in a forward P/E less than the trailing P/E. If the earnings growth forecast was negative, the forward P/E would be greater, not smaller (as in the vignette), as the forward P/E denominator would be smaller than the trailing P/E denominator.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because the numerator (current stock price) is the same in both the trailing and forward P/E ratios.

questions.module: Market-Based Valuation: Price and Enterprise Value Multiples
questions.los: Normalized EPS via the average ROE method
questions.stem: Xita's normalized EPS based on the average ROE method is closest to:

explanations.B: See correct answer C.
explanations.C: C is correct because in the method of average return on equity normalized EPS is calculated as the average return on equity (ROE) from the most recent full cycle, multiplied by current book value per share. Each year's ROE is computed by dividing EPS by BVPS, giving ROE values, by year, of: Year 1: 3.19/10.90 = 29.3%; Year 2: 2.21/12.50 =17.7%; Year 3: 0.37/12.60 = 2.9%; Year 4: 2.56/13.30 =19.2%. questions.module: Market-Based Valuation: Price and Enterprise Value Multiples
questions.los: Choosing an appropriate multiple (EV/Sales) given capital structure and intangibles
questions.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate metric for Albertson to use in valuing Garc?

explanations.A: A is incorrect as dividend yield is only one component of total return; not using all information related to expected return is suboptimal. With growth opportunities arising in the industry, capital gains are likely to be an important source of future returns. In addition, the investment required to capitalize on the growth opportunities may adversely affect Garc's ability to pay dividends in the future – especially because Garc's dividend payout ratio is the highest in the industry, which is attractive to many of its current investors. A useful metric in assessing the safety of the dividend is the payout ratio: A high payout relative to other companies operating in the same industry may indicate a less secure dividend because the dividend is less well covered by earnings.
explanations.B: B is incorrect as a material portion of Garc's value arises from the value of its brand, which as an internally generated intangible asset is not shown on the balance sheet (and thus not reflected in book value per share). Assets in addition to those recognized in financial statements may be critical operating factors. For example, in many service companies, human capital—the value of skills and knowledge possessed by the workforce—is more important than physical capital as an operating factor, but it is not reflected as an asset on the balance sheet. In addition, accounting effects on book value may compromise how useful book value is as a measure of the shareholders’ investment in the company. In general, intangible assets that are generated internally (as opposed to being acquired) are not shown as assets on a company’s balance sheet. For example, companies account for advertising and marketing as expenses, so the value of internally generated brands, which are created and maintained by advertising and marketing activities, do not appear as assets on a company’s balance sheet under IFRS or US GAAP.
explanations.C: C is correct because the numerator of the EV/Sales ratio is the firm's total value of debt and equity. EV/S is an alternative sales-based ratio that is particularly useful when comparing companies with diverse capital structures, which applies to Garc's industry. Sales is an appropriate denominator as sales growth is consistent and not as variable as earnings. In addition, sales are generally less subject to distortion or manipulation than are other fundamentals, such as EPS or book value.

questions.module: Market-Based Valuation: Price and Enterprise Value Multiples
questions.los: Relative strength technical indicator vs. an index
questions.stem: Garc's relative strength compared to the market index over the past year is closest to:

explanations.A: A is correct because the relative strength measure of Garc against the market index is 1.0154. The value of Garc divided by the index at the beginning of the period is 27.95 / 550.40 = 0.050781; the relative strength on that day is thus 0.050781 / 0.050781 = 1.0000. At the end of the time frame, the value of Garc divided by the index is 31.05 / 602.21 = 0.051560. Thus, over the time frame the relative strength measure for Garc is 0.051560 / 0.050781 = 1.0153. Dividends are not incorporated into the relative strength calculation because relative strength is based strictly on price movement. Also, the valuation indicators we call momentum indicators relate either price or a fundamental, such as earnings, to the time series of their own past values. A simple relative-strength indicator of the second type (i.e., the stock’s performance relative to the performance of some group of stocks) is the stock’s performance divided by the performance of an equity index. If the value of this ratio increases, the stock price increases relative to the index and displays positive relative strength.
explanations.B: See correct answer A.
explanations.C: See correct answer A.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: Relative strength = (stock/index at end) ÷ (stock/index at start); price only, dividends excluded

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: Relative strength uses PRICES only — ignore the $1.24 dividend and the index dividend yield.

questions.los: Net stable funding ratio drivers (CAMELS liquidity)
questions.stem: An increase in which of the following would best explain the trend in Sigmar's net stable funding ratio?

explanations.A: A is incorrect because an increase in loans to customers (a component of the bank's asset base) would be consistent with a decrease, not an increase, in the NSFR.
explanations.B: B is correct because the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) is expressed as the minimum percentage of a bank’s required stable funding that must be sourced from available stable funding. For this ratio, required stable funding (the denominator) is a function of the composition and maturity of a bank’s asset base, whereas available stable funding (the numerator) is a function of the composition and maturity of a bank’s funding sources (i.e., capital and deposits and other liabilities). The NSFR has steadily increased over the past three years. Accordingly, an increase in long-term debt liabilities (a funding source) would be consistent with an increase in the NSFR.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because highly liquid assets do not enter the calculation of the Net Stable Funding Ratio.

explanations.B: B is incorrect because Sigmar follows US GAAP, so a difference in share price between the settlement date and the grant date will cause income tax expense to increase or decrease.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because a lower (not higher) share price at settlement versus at the grant date results in a lower tax deduction than the cumulative stock-based compensation expense.

questions.los: Choosing a valuation model for a negative-earnings asset-rich firm

explanations.A: A is correct because Globac has significant iron ore reserves. Asset-based valuation would be a better fit given the company is struggling financially and the value of the company will be derived from its assets (in this case iron ore reserves). Asset-based valuation values a company on the basis of the market value of the assets or resources it controls. Hence, the method is a reasonable approach.

A relative valuation model estimates an asset’s value relative to that of another asset. The idea underlying relative valuation is that similar assets should sell at similar prices.

An increase in leverage will not affect FCFF (although it might affect the calculations used to arrive at FCFF). An increase in leverage affects FCFE in two ways. In the year the debt is issued, it increases the FCFE by the amount of debt issued. After the debt is issued, FCFE is then reduced by the after-tax interest expense. questions.module: Market-Based Valuation: Price and Enterprise Value Multiples
questions.los: Choosing a stable multiple (P/S) given intangibles and earnings distortion
questions.stem: Which of the following valuation ratios is most suitable for Kassam to value Altair?

explanations.A: A is incorrect because one of the possible drawbacks of the P/B is its inability to capture critical operating assets required in addition to those recognized in financial statements. Intangible assets that are generated internally (as opposed to being acquired) are not shown as assets on a company’s balance sheet. For example, companies account for advertising and marketing as expenses, so the value of internally generated brands, which are created and maintained by advertising and marketing activities, do not appear as assets on a company’s balance sheet under IFRS or US GAAP. Accounting effects such as these may impair the comparability of P/B among companies unless appropriate analyst adjustments are made – hence, it will not be the most suitable indicator for Kassam to use.
explanations.B: B is correct because Kassam wants to use a stable multiple without making any considerable adjustments to reported financials, P/S is a suitable multiple. Sales are generally less subject to distortion or manipulation than are other fundamentals, such as EPS or book value and because sales are generally more stable than EPS, which reflects operating and financial leverage, P/S is generally more stable than P/E.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because earnings are more prone to manipulation due to discretionary accounting decision about expenses which can distort EPS as a reflection of economic performance. Hence, such distortions may affect the comparability of P/Es among companies and will not be the most suitable indicator for Kassam to use without making any adjustments.

questions.los: Excess earnings method
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 3, the value of Becq using the excess earnings method is closest to:

explanations.A: See correct answer B.
explanations.B: B is correct because the valuation using the excess earnings method involves estimating earnings remaining after deducting amounts that reflect the required returns on working capital and fixed assets (i.e., the tangible assets). This residual amount of earnings (i.e., “excess earnings”) is capitalized by using the growing perpetuity formula from the CCM to obtain an estimate of the value of intangible assets. For valuing the entire business, the values of working capital and fixed assets are added to the capitalized value of intangibles. Required return on working capital (315,000 × 3.25%) = 10,237.50. Required return on fixed assets (725,000 × 8.50%) = 61,625.00. Residual earnings (191,290 – 10,237.50 – 61,625) = 119,427.50. Value of intangible assets 119,427.50 × (1 + 2.50%)/(11.25% – 2.50%) = 1,399,008. Total value of the company (1,399,008 + 315,000 + 725,000) = 2,439,007.86 (closest to 2,440,000).
explanations.C: See correct answer B.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: Excess earnings = earnings – return on WC – return on FA; capitalize via growing perpetuity, then add WC + FA

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: Capitalize the EXCESS earnings (not total earnings), then add back the tangible WC and FA to value the whole business.

questions.module: Valuation and Analysis of Bonds with Embedded Options
questions.los: Valuing a callable bond on a binomial tree
questions.stem: Based on the binomial interest rate tree, the value of Bond A is closest to:

explanations.A: A is correct because we start at the end of the tree and work backwards to determine the value at each node recognizing that if the value is greater than 100, it is optimal to call the bond at par (i.e., it is optimal to call the bond at par if the future 1-year rate is less than the coupon of 5%). Because this is a 2-year bond, the relevant rates to use are the Year 0 (2%) and Year 1 rates (4.08% and 6.09%). We start at the end of the interest rate tree, where the bond makes a payment of 105 (principal plus coupon). Interest rates at Year 1 are 6.09% and 4.08% and Year 1 values are computed as follows: At a rate of 6.09%, the bond value is 105/1.0609 = 98.97. At a rate of 4.08%, the value would be 105/1.0408 = 100.88 and the bond would be called at its par value of 100. Year 1 values are then 98.97 and 100. Working backwards to Year 0, with a rate of 2%, we discount the Year 1 values (plus the $5 coupon) to arrive at two values: (100 + 5)/1.02 = 102.9412; (98.97 + 5)/1.02 = 101.9339. With equal probabilities, the value at Year 0 is then the equally weighted average which is 102.4375 or 102.44.
explanations.B: See correct answer A.
explanations.C: See correct answer A.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: Backward-induct; at each Year-1 node, if the value > 100 the issuer calls, so cap value at 100 (call when rate < 5% coupon)

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: Issuer's call caps the node value at 100 (the opposite of a put); add the $5 coupon at each node before discounting at 2%.

questions.module: Valuation and Analysis of Bonds with Embedded Options
questions.los: Effective convexity of a putable bond cannot be negative
questions.stem: The effective convexity of Bond B:

choices.B: will become negative if the rate in Year 1 is less than the bond's coupon.
choices.C: will become negative if the rate in Year 1 is greater than the bond's coupon.

explanations.A: A is correct because an option-free bond has positive convexity, and the addition of the right to put the bond back to the issuing firm reinforces this. Consequently, the convexity of Bond B which is a putable bond cannot be negative.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because unlike a callable bond, the putable bond B cannot have an effective convexity that is negative. If the Year 1 rate is less than the coupon, the bond would sell at a premium and the put option would not be exercised, effectively making the bond behave like a straight bond (that would have positive convexity).
explanations.C: C is incorrect because unlike a callable bond, the putable bond B cannot have an effective convexity that is negative. If the Year 1 rate is greater than the coupon, the put option would be in the money and simply provides a floor for its price without affecting the upside price appreciation.

questions.module: Valuation and Analysis of Bonds with Embedded Options
questions.los: Effect of higher volatility on a callable bond's OAS
questions.stem: Under Plessinger's scenario, the OAS of the corporate bond will:

explanations.A: A is correct because under her scenario Plessinger assumes an increase in interest rate volatility (from 20% to 25%) which will lead to a decrease in the callable bond's OAS. We can see this by examining the bond's Z-spread. At zero volatility, the OAS is the Z-spread. For a bond with an embedded option, the Z-spread will capture differences in credit risk, liquidity and optionality relative to the benchmark curve. Increasing the interest rate volatility will increase the value of the embedded option and since we keep the bond price fixed (Z-spread is fixed too), the remaining spread (i.e., the OAS) must decline since Z-spread = OAS + option cost. The OAS is the spread remaining adjusted for the cost of the option.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because an increase in the assumed interest rate volatility leads to a decrease in the OAS for the callable bond.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because an increase in the assumed interest rate volatility leads to a decrease in the OAS for the callable bond.

questions.module: Valuation and Analysis of Bonds with Embedded Options
questions.los: Valuing a capped floating-rate bond
questions.stem: The value of the capped floating rate bond analyzed by Plessinger is:

explanations.A: A is correct because the capped floater will have its rate limited to 5% and there are instances where the rate could be greater than 5%. The case text states the following: The floater's coupon pays the one-year reference rate annually, set in arrears, and is capped at 5.0%. To evaluate the default-free capped floater we must look at the exhibit that shows the evolution of 1-year rates based on a volatility of 20% and the spot rates from the exhibit. There are two instances where the cap would be in force; in Year 1 if rates are 6.09% and in Year 2 if rates are 7.32%. In both of these instances the floating rate bond will have a value less than its par value of 100. Working backwards, we will arrive at a value less than 100. In the absence of the cap, the floating rate bond would sell at par at each annual reset date.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because there are cases where the cap will be in effect and as a result the floating rate bond will sell for less than its par value. While the spot rates in the exhibit are all less than the 5% cap, it is the evolution of 1-year rates in the binomial interest rate tree that is used to evaluate the cap and in this case there are rates which exceed the cap.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because in this case, the capped floating rate bond cannot sell for more than its par value. With the presence of the 5% cap, the capped floater will sell for less than its par value.

questions.los: Choosing FCFF three-stage for changing capital structure
questions.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate approach to use for valuing Firm A?

explanations.A: A is incorrect because earnings growth follows a three-stage model and FCFF is preferred over FCFE when capital structure is expected to change. Three stages: Since Firm A's earnings will go through a period of gradual decline between the high growth phase and stable growth phase, the overall growth regime is best characterized with three stages. FCFF: FCFE is not appropriate when capital structure is expected to change. For Firm A, highly fluctuating amounts of net borrowing is expected due to primarily debt-financed aggressive growth strategy. Therefore, FCFF is more appropriate than FCFE.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because FCFE is not appropriate when capital structure is expected to change. For Firm A, highly fluctuating amounts of net borrowing is expected due to primarily debt-financed aggressive growth strategy. Therefore, FCFF is more appropriate than FCFE.
explanations.C: C is correct because earnings growth follows a three-stage model and FCFF is preferred over FCFE when capital structure is expected to change. Three stages: A common model is a three-stage model with constant growth rates in Stages 1 and 3 and a declining growth rate in Stage 2. Since Firm A's earnings will go through a period of gradual decline between the high growth phase and stable growth phase, the overall growth regime is best characterized with three stages. 1) Stage 1 (high growth stage): Next three years characterized 25%-35% annual growth. 2) Stage 2 (declining growth stage): Period where annual growth rate declines to stable growth level of 2%. 3) Stage 3 (stable growth stage): Time period where annual growth rate is stabilized at the long-term sustainable rate of 2%. In addition, three-stage models are often considered to be good approximations for cash flow streams that, in reality, fluctuate from year to year. Consistently, McCormick's expectations suggest that Firm A's earnings are expected to fluctuate due to the management's aggressive growth strategy. FCFF: Finally, if a company’s capital structure is relatively stable, using FCFE to value equity is more direct and simpler than using FCFF. The FCFF model is often chosen, however, in two other cases: [1] A levered company with negative FCFE and [2] A levered company with a changing capital structure. For Firm A, highly fluctuating amounts of net borrowing is expected due to primarily debt-financed aggressive growth strategy. Therefore, FCFF is more appropriate than FCFE.

questions.los: FCFE from CFO
questions.stem: Firm B's FCFE (in $ millions) is closest to:

explanations.A: See correct answer C.
explanations.B: See correct answer C.
explanations.C: C is correct because Free cash flow to equity (FCFE) can be calculated starting from cash flow from operations (CFO). FCFE = CFO – FCInv + Net borrowing where, CFO: Cash flow from operations = 535; FCInv: Investment in fixed capital = 110; Net borrowing = 65. FCFE = 535 – 110 + 65 = 490.

steps.label: 公式

questions.los: Share issuance does not affect FCFE
questions.stem: Given Firm C's announced change, next year's FCFE forecast will most likely:

explanations.A: A is incorrect because next year's FCFE will not be affected by the common stock issuance. This is because transactions between the company and its shareholders (through cash dividends, share repurchases, and share issuances) do not affect free cash flow.
explanations.B: B is correct because transactions between the company and its shareholders (through cash dividends, share repurchases, and share issuances) do not affect free cash flow. Transactions that involve exchanging cash flows between the firm and shareholders represent the use of FCFE whereas FCFE represents cash flows available to stockholders and is irrelevant to how firm uses its FCFE.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because next year's FCFE will not be affected by the common stock issuance. This is because transactions between the company and its shareholders (through cash dividends, share repurchases, and share issuances) do not affect free cash flow.

questions.los: Equity value from FCFF (add non-operating, subtract debt and preferred)
questions.stem: The intrinsic value of Firm D's equity based on FCFF approach is closest to:

explanations.A: See correct answer B.
explanations.B: B is correct because the intrinsic value of Firm D's equity based on the FCFF approach can be calculated as: Intrinsic value of the equity = Value of operating assets + Value of non-operating assets – Market value of debt – Market value of preferred stock where, Value of operating assets = present value of future FCFF = $800 million; Value of non-operating assets = $75 million; Market value of debt = $250 million; Market value of preferred stock = $150 million. Intrinsic value of the equity = 800 + 75 – 250 – 150 = $475 million.
explanations.C: See correct answer B.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: Equity value = PV(FCFF) + non-operating assets – MV(debt) – MV(preferred)

steps.label: 结果
steps.content: = $475 million

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: Add back the $75m excess (non-operating) cash, then subtract BOTH debt and preferred stock from firm value.

questions.los: Sustainable sales growth: organic (volume + price) vs. currency
questions.stem: The market with the highest sustainable sales growth rate is:

explanations.A: A is incorrect because growth in sales from volume was only 5 percent and price was 0 percent. Growth in net sales was strongly contributed by changes in exchange rate (4 percent). Growth in sales that comes from changes in volume or price is arguably more sustainable than growth in sales that comes from changes in exchange rates.
explanations.B: B is correct because the growth in sales for Malaysia came from change in volume and price. At 4 + 5 = 9 percent, the organic sales growth was the greatest compared to Thailand (5 + 0 = 5) or Hong Kong SAR (–4 + 8 = 4). Growth in sales that comes from changes in volume or price is arguably more sustainable than growth in sales that comes from changes in exchange rates.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because overall sustainable sales growth was 4 percent. Growth in price was the highest at 8 percent, while growth in sales from volume was –4 percent. Thus, overall sustainable sales growth was 8 – 4 = 4 percent. This is lower than the 9 percent reported in Malaysia.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: Sustainable (organic) sales growth = volume growth + price growth (exclude currency effect)

steps.label: 代入
steps.content: Thailand: 5 + 0 = 5%; Malaysia: 4 + 5 = 9%; Hong Kong SAR: –4 + 8 = 4%

steps.label: 结果
steps.content: Malaysia has the highest organic growth at 9%

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: Exclude the foreign-currency component; currency-driven growth (e.g., Thailand's 4%) is not sustainable.

questions.los: Temporal method: translation gain/loss with net monetary liability
questions.stem: For the most recent year, as a result of consolidating Creamy's results, Buttery would recognize a:

choices.A: translation loss in the income statement.
choices.B: translation gain in the income statement.
choices.C: negative translation adjustment in the balance sheet.

explanations.A: A is correct because Creamy had a net monetary liability position and the IDR strengthened against the USD. Using the temporal method, a foreign currency translation loss is recognized in the income statement under these conditions.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because Creamy had a net monetary liability position and the IDR strengthened against the USD. Using the temporal method, a foreign currency translation loss, not gain, is recognized in the income statement under these conditions.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because Creamy had a net monetary liability position and the IDR strengthened against the USD. Using the temporal method, a foreign currency translation loss is recognized in the income statement, not a negative translation adjustment in the balance sheet under these conditions.

questions.los: Temporal method: which ratio is unchanged after translation
questions.stem: Which of the following ratios for Creamy most likely remains unchanged after translation for the most recent year?

explanations.A: A is incorrect because current ratio = current assets / current liabilities and the numerator and denominator are translated using different exchange rates. Current assets comprise both monetary assets (cash, receivables) and non-monetary assets (inventory) and current liabilities tend to be monetary in nature. Most liabilities are monetary liabilities. Under the temporal method, monetary assets and liabilities are translated at the year end rate of 14,000. Inventory is a non-monetary asset and it is translated using the weighted average historical exchange rate when purchased or 14,700. This changes the numerator after translation. The denominator which is current liabilities are mostly monetary and translated at the year end rate of 14,000. Accordingly, the current ratio after translation changes. Inventory is translated at the historical exchange rate under the temporal method.
explanations.B: B is correct because both the numerator and denominator are translated at the same rate resulting in the translated ratio being the same as the ratio in local currency. Under the temporal method, sales is translated using the average rate and COGS is translated at the historical exchange rate that inventory was purchased. Both the average rate and the weighted average historical rate when inventory was purchased rate are 14,700. The numerator and denominator are translated at the same rate. Accordingly, the translated ratio is the same as the ratio calculated using the local currency. Cost of goods sold is translated using the exchange rates that existed when the inventory items assumed to have been sold during the year were acquired.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because the numerator and denominator are translated using different exchange rates. Under the temporal method, sales (the numerator) is translated using the average rate of 14,700. Receivables (the denominator) are monetary assets and translated at the year end rate of 14,000. Accordingly, the ratio after translation changes and is different from the ratio calculated using the local currency.

questions.los: IAS 29 restatement of non-monetary items in hyperinflation
questions.stem: If Tay's expectation is correct, when translating Dairy's current year financial statements, Buttery is required to restate Dairy's:

explanations.A: A is correct because non-monetary assets are restated for changes in the general purchasing power of the monetary unit and then the inflation adjusted statements are translated using the current exchange rate. IFRS require the foreign currency financial statements first to be restated for inflation using the procedures of IAS 29. The restated cost is determined by applying to the historical cost the change in the general price index from the date of acquisition to the balance sheet date. Since inventory is carried at historical cost, the restated cost is determined by applying to the historical cost the change in the general price index from the date of acquisition to the balance sheet date before translation.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because under IAS 29, monetary items (such as cash, accounts receivable and accounts payable) are not restated because they are already expressed in terms of the monetary unit current at the balance sheet date.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because under IAS 29, monetary items (such as cash, accounts receivables and accounts payable) are not restated because they are already expressed in terms of the monetary unit current at the balance sheet date.

questions.module: The Term Structure and Interest Rate Dynamics
questions.los: Term structure theories: segmented markets
questions.stem: Li's observations about the shape of the yield curve are most consistent with the:

explanations.A: A is incorrect because Li’s view of the market is not supported by the preferred habitat theory. Under the preferred habitat theory, investors will strongly prefer to transact within a defined maturity range, but if yields are sufficiently attractive outside that range, they will migrate to the alternative maturities.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because Li’s view of the market is not supported by the liquidity preference theory. Under the liquidity preference theory, forward rates are not unbiased estimates of future spot rates, because investors expect to earn a liquidity premium that increases the farther out on the yield curve they go. The liquidity preference theory is inconsistent with borrower and lender preferences influencing the shape of the yield curve.
explanations.C: C is correct because Li’s view of the market is supported by the segmented markets theory. This theory assumes that investors access the bond market only in specific maturity ranges, and will not move outside those ranges even if yields become more attractive in alternative maturities.

questions.module: The Term Structure and Interest Rate Dynamics
questions.los: Forward rate framework: valuation when future spot < forward
questions.stem: Given his forecast, Li should consider a 5-year zero-coupon bond today to be:

explanations.A: A is correct because if Li’s forecast is correct, bond cash flows are currently being discounted at higher rates than the rates that will be used to discount them in the future, so 5-year bonds are currently undervalued. The current bond value is based on the implied forward rate observed for those final two years, and the bond's value will be higher if that two-year rate is lower in the future.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because a bond will be fairly valued today only if future spot rates equal implied forward rates calculated using today's yield curve. In this case, future spot rates are forecasted to be lower than implied forward rates, which means bond cash flows are presently being discounted at too high a rate, producing a price that is low relative to fair value.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because a bond will be overvalued today only if future spot rates exceed implied forward rates calculated using today's yield curve. In this case, future spot rates are forecasted to be lower than implied forward rates, which means bond cash flows are presently being discounted at too high a rate, producing a price that is low relative to fair value.

questions.module: The Term Structure and Interest Rate Dynamics
questions.los: Riding the yield curve: buy maturity longer than horizon
questions.stem: To implement the strategy for Client A, Li should buy a:

explanations.A: A is incorrect because riding the yield curve involves buying securities with maturities that are greater than the investor’s investment horizon. In this case, the investment horizon is two years, so buying a one-year security would not be correct.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because riding the yield curve involves buying securities with maturities that are greater than the investor’s investment horizon. In this case, the investment horizon is two years, so buying a two-year security would not be correct.
explanations.C: C is correct because riding the yield curve involves buying securities with maturities that are greater than the investor’s investment horizon. In this case, the investment horizon is two years, and the correct security to purchase has a three-year maturity. When the yield curve is upward sloping (as in Exhibit 1) and the investor does not expect a change in its level or shape, conditions are favorable for this strategy. The investor buys a security with a longer maturity than the investment horizon, and sells when the investment horizon date is reached. Assuming an upward-sloping yield curve, the passage of time causes the yield on the bond to decrease, which provides extra return to the investor.

questions.module: The Term Structure and Interest Rate Dynamics
questions.los: Annualizing yield volatility; key rate duration vs. volatility term structure
questions.stem: Are Li's calculation and conclusion related to key rate duration and term structure volatility correct?

choices.B: No, only his annualized volatility estimate is correct
choices.C: No, only his conclusion related to key rate duration and term structure volatility is correct

explanations.A: A is incorrect because although the annualized volatility estimate is calculated correctly, the statement about key rate duration and yield curve volatility is incorrect.
explanations.B: B is correct because the monthly standard deviation of yield curve volatility can be annualized by multiplying it by the square root of 12. So, 3.25% ×12^(1/2) ≈11.26%.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because while it is true that longer-term securities have higher key rate durations, the volatility term structure typically shows that short-term rates are more volatile than long-term rates. Key rate duration measures the effect on a bond's price of a change in yield at a particular point on the yield curve. However, key rate duration does not measure the propensity of rates at different maturities to be volatile.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: Annualized yield volatility = monthly standard deviation × √12; key rate duration ≠ measure of rate volatility

steps.label: 结果
steps.content: Volatility estimate is correct, but the KRD conclusion is wrong → answer B

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: Short-term rates are typically MORE volatile than long-term rates; high KRD does not imply high term-structure volatility.

questions.los: SPE consolidation under IFRS (control) and debt-to-assets
questions.stem: Acme's consolidated debt-to-assets ratio would most likely be:

choices.A: lower under Option 1 compared to Option 2.
choices.B: the same under either Option 1 or Option 2.
choices.C: higher under Option 1 compared to Option 2.

explanations.A: A is incorrect because Acme has the ability to influence the financial and operating policy of the SPE and will absorb any losses the SPE may incur, and is thus exposed to variable returns from the SPE. Therefore, the consolidated balance sheet (of Acme) would look exactly the same as if it borrowed directly against the receivables.
explanations.B: B is correct because IFRS require consolidation if the substance of the relationship indicates control by the sponsor. Under IFRS 10, Consolidated Financial Statements and SIC-12, Consolidation-Special Purpose Entities, the definition of control extends to a broad range of activities. The control concept requires judgment and evaluation of relevant factors to determine whether control exists. Control is present when 1) the investor has the ability to exert influence on the financial and operating policy of the entity; and 2) is exposed, or has rights, to variable returns from its involvement with the investee. Acme has the ability to influence the financial and operating policy of the SPE and will absorb any losses the SPE may incur, and is thus exposed to variable returns from the SPE. Therefore, the consolidated balance sheet (of Acme) would look exactly the same as if it borrowed directly against the receivables.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because IFRS require consolidation if the substance of the relationship indicates control by the sponsor. Acme has the ability to influence the financial and operating policy of the SPE and will absorb any losses the SPE may incur, and is thus exposed to variable returns from the SPE. Therefore, the consolidated balance sheet (of Acme) would look exactly the same as if it borrowed directly against the receivables.
